project_type: Two-sided online marketplace (SaaS) with virtual currency, subscription billing and affiliate programme
project_description: A book-review marketplace where self-published authors list books and pay in a virtual currency called Quills, and readers apply to review those books and earn Quills back. Quills are purchased with real money via Stripe subscriptions and one-off top-up packs. The platform includes an affiliate/referral programme with commissions and payouts, a support and dispute desk, an admin back office with analytics and editable pricing rules, and a full per-action audit trail. It is a ground-up rebuild of an earlier Quillva system retained in the repository as old-build/.

workflows: Author listing lifecycle: book submit -> admin approval -> listing with rules-engine pricing -> Quill debit -> optional delayed publish -> reviewer applications -> reviews -> author confirmation -> reviewer credit -> refund on cancel/delete
Reviewer application lifecycle: browse with country/mutual-review/cap filters -> apply -> 7-day due date -> TTL-bounded reminder -> review or auto-expiry -> Quill grant or revocation
Billing lifecycle: checkout -> trial -> trial credit -> invoice.paid allocation -> payment failure 7-day grace -> refund/dispute reversal and restore
Affiliate lifecycle: referral code -> tokenised link -> hashed click tracking -> attribution -> commission accrual -> payout request and review
Support lifecycle: ticket -> threaded messages with admin read receipts -> linked Stripe dispute -> resolution

engineering_challenges.challenge: Reversible money in a two-currency system
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Stripe can deliver the same event twice, out of order, and months apart; a dispute produces two opposite ledger effects. A replayed event and a re-derived effect are different failures requiring different defences.
engineering_challenges.solution: Event-ID dedup table plus deterministic unique per-effect idempotency keys, with a distinct restore key for dispute-won.

engineering_challenges.why_hard: Cron inside the API means every replica runs every job; scaling the API silently multiplies side effects.
engineering_challenges.solution: Extracted a separate worker service AND made every job row-level idempotent via compare-and-set, so correctness never depended on single-instance execution.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Cross-site cookie auth behind a proxy chain
engineering_challenges.why_hard: SameSite, Secure, cookie domain and Express trust proxy interact across Netlify -> Cloudflare -> NGINX -> Render; the failure mode is a silent 401 with no server-side error and no local reproduction.
engineering_challenges.solution: Empirical bisection across 14 deployable increments, converging on trust proxy enabled, no forced domain, minimal JWT payload.

engineering_challenges.challenge: At-least-once delivery meeting a must-happen-once side effect
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Sending an email twice is user-visible. Queue configuration limits blast radius but provides no exactly-once guarantee.
engineering_challenges.solution: Atomic conditional UPDATE acting as a distributed lock; TTL and DLX as backstops.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Timezone correctness for a third party's clock
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Listings publish on Amazon's schedule, not the server's or the user's; the failure only surfaces as 'it went live late'.
engineering_challenges.solution: Luxon zone conversion rather than Date arithmetic; production fix correcting America/Los_Angeles to America/New_York.

decisions.problem: Cron inside the API couples job execution to HTTP deployment and duplicates jobs per replica
decisions.decision: Extract worker.ts/worker.module.ts, deploy as a separate Render worker from the same image, gated by LISTING_SCHEDULER_WORKER
decisions.reasoning: Written out in TODOS.md with an explicit trigger condition
decisions.tradeoffs: A second service to deploy, monitor and pay for; shared image means a backend deploy redeploys both
decisions.result: API restarts no longer pause background work; scaling no longer risks duplicate jobs

decisions.problem: Two different temporal needs: fan-out reminders versus single future-dated publications
decisions.decision: RabbitMQ with DLX/TTL for reminders; BullMQ delayed jobs with deterministic job IDs for publication
decisions.reasoning: INFERRED from code shape - BullMQ jobId+delay makes reschedule-by-replace trivial; RabbitMQ DLX/TTL makes expiring stale work trivial
decisions.tradeoffs: Two brokers to run and reason about, unusual for a system of this size
decisions.result: Both work, at the cost of operational surface area

decisions.problem: 15 categories of pricing input, changed frequently
decisions.decision: QuillRule table with category/key/min/max/value read at estimate time
decisions.reasoning: Avoid a deploy per pricing experiment
decisions.tradeoffs: Pricing logic is no longer type-checked or PR-reviewed; a bad admin edit is a production incident with no rollback
decisions.result: 91 live rules; economics change without deploys

decisions.problem: Env-var Stripe price IDs require a redeploy to change and lose the record of what past customers paid
decisions.decision: BillingPriceMapping with validFrom/validTo, isActive and quillsSnapshot, bootstrapped idempotently on each deploy
decisions.tradeoffs: One more source of truth to keep in sync with the Stripe dashboard
decisions.result: 17 mappings, 11 active; superseded prices retained rather than overwritten

decisions.problem: A failed invoice originally cut access immediately, punishing users with an expired card
decisions.decision: Set Stripe cancel_at to now + 7 days and email the customer, letting dunning retries run
decisions.tradeoffs: Up to 7 days of unpaid access
decisions.result: 101 production payment-failure events handled as a grace window rather than instant lockout

decisions.problem: Account deletion would destroy financial and review history
decisions.tradeoffs: Every query must filter deletedAt; the unique email constraint had to become composite [email, deletedAt]
decisions.result: History preserved; re-registration after deletion still works

lessons: Absence of a derived record is not absence of the source event. I wrongly concluded this platform had no paying customers because no Quill-credit ledger entries existed for paid invoices - but the BASIC plan allocates zero Quills, so the ledger was correctly silent. The chargebacks were the disconfirming evidence available all along: a chargeback cannot exist without a charge.
Go to the failing call, not the error message - the legacy webhook bug was invisible from its symptoms and obvious at the constructEvent call site.
Never trust debug output you did not write; fabricated certainty is worse than no information.
A fallback that hides a failure is worse than the failure - req.rawBody || req.body || req was written as a safety net and worked as a blindfold.
Idempotency belongs in the database, not the queue - every guarantee that held in production is a unique constraint or a conditional update.
Two independent dedup layers are not redundancy: event-level and effect-level keys catch genuinely different failures, as the dispute-restore case proves.
Empirical debugging is the right tool for opaque infrastructure; a messy git log can be the correct trade-off.
Configuration the business changes often should live in the database - but it also needs validity windows and value snapshots, or you lose the history of what customers paid.
Invest test coverage where money moves; but leaving 33 scaffold specs in place misrepresents coverage, and deleting them would have been more honest.
Separating the worker was right; doing it earlier would have been better. The risk was written down before it was fixed, which means it was understood and deferred rather than missed.
What I would change: CI on every push; error tracking before launch; one broker instead of two; explicit migration step rather than prisma db seed in pre-deploy.

interview_stories.title: The fallback that became a blindfold
interview_stories.situation: A long-standing client's platform, built by another team, had a Stripe webhook that would not verify signatures. The team had been stuck and AI tooling had not resolved it.
interview_stories.task: Diagnose a payment defect in a codebase I had never seen, for a client who had lost confidence in the delivery.
interview_stories.action: Went to the signature-verification call rather than the symptom. Found a fallback chain passing parsed JSON into constructEvent whenever the raw body was missing - guaranteeing failure and suppressing the signal. Then found a second bug in their own debug logging whose signature comparison could never return true, which is almost certainly why they and their AI tools kept chasing the secret instead of the input.
interview_stories.result: Fixed within a few hours of first touching the code.
interview_stories.evidence: Both defects remain in old-build/backend/src/webhook/webhook.controller.ts; the rebuild replaces the class of problem with one line of raw-body middleware.
interview_stories.why_it_lands: It is a story about reading the failing call rather than the error message, and about not trusting debug output you did not write.

interview_stories.title: Saying no to a launch
interview_stories.situation: After the fix, the client asked whether the platform was ready to go live. The easy, profitable answer was yes.
interview_stories.action: Reviewed authentication, the payment path and the frontend. Found no webhook idempotency, origin:'*' CORS with a comment admitting it was insecure, the webhook secret logged on every failure, six overlapping UI libraries, two state libraries, two payment providers, and no type safety or meaningful tests. Advised against launch and proposed a rebuild, framing the financial risk for a non-technical owner rather than listing code smells.
interview_stories.result: The client accepted; the rebuild shipped and went live in June 2026.
interview_stories.why_it_lands: The rebuild was the proportionate call, not the ambitious one.

interview_stories.title: The cookie that wouldn't stick
interview_stories.situation: SPA on Netlify, API on Render behind Cloudflare/NGINX; auth succeeded but every subsequent request returned 401, with no local reproduction.
interview_stories.task: Make httpOnly cookie auth work cross-origin.
interview_stories.action: Added token-generation logging, then bisected the SameSite/Secure/domain/trust-proxy matrix across 14 small deployable increments in one day.
interview_stories.result: Auth worked; 3,488 GET /auth/me calls follow in production logs.

interview_stories.title: The chargeback that had to reverse twice
interview_stories.situation: Stripe can deliver the same event twice, out of order, months apart; a duplicate credit is real money lost.
interview_stories.task: Make the Quill ledger provably correct under replay.
interview_stories.action: Built two independent layers - an event-ID dedup table and deterministic unique idempotency keys per ledger effect, with separate keys for a dispute's debit and its restore-on-win.
interview_stories.result: 462 production events, 462 distinct IDs, no double-credit.
interview_stories.evidence: webhook.service.ts; schema unique constraint; production query

interview_stories.title: The worker that should have been separate sooner
interview_stories.situation: Cron and BullMQ ran inside the API, so every replica would duplicate every job.
interview_stories.task: Decide whether to fix it now or ship features.
interview_stories.action: Wrote the trade-off into TODOS.md with an explicit trigger condition, shipped features, extracted worker.ts as its own Render service when the risk became real, and made every job row-level idempotent.
interview_stories.result: API restarts no longer pause background work.

interview_stories.title: The duplicate accounts
interview_stories.situation: Case-sensitive email matching split Quill balances and Stripe customers across duplicate accounts.
interview_stories.task: Fix the cause and repair live data without destroying anything.
interview_stories.action: Reference-count scoring to decide what was safe to delete, dry-run by default with explicit --apply, a merge script with a reviewed plan per pair, and a source-level fix.

interview_stories.title: Where I spent my test budget
interview_stories.situation: Solo engineer, broad feature surface, limited time.
interview_stories.action: Wrote real tests only for the Stripe service and webhook service - refund reversal, dispute debit, dispute restore.
interview_stories.result: The money paths are covered; the rest is not.
interview_stories.evidence: Spec file audit: 35 files, 9 real tests, 33 NestJS scaffolds
interview_stories.self_critique: I'd defend the allocation and criticise the execution - leaving scaffold specs in place misrepresents coverage.

interview_stories.title: Pricing out of code
interview_stories.situation: Quill pricing depended on word count, channel, country, media and caps, and changed often.
interview_stories.action: Moved it into a rules table read at estimate time; later did the same for Stripe price IDs, but with validity windows and snapshots after learning that overwriting a price loses the record of what past customers paid.
interview_stories.result: 91 rules and 17 mappings live, changeable without a deploy.
interview_stories.tradeoff_to_raise: Pricing logic is no longer type-checked or PR-reviewed, and a bad admin edit is an incident with no rollback.

portfolio_material.positioning: A two-sided marketplace where real money, a virtual currency and deadline-driven workflows all have to stay reconciled - built and operated solo.
portfolio_material.challenge: Money that can flow backwards; economics that change weekly; a workflow driven by deadlines rather than clicks; a legacy stack to replace on a small-team budget.
portfolio_material.role: Sole backend engineer and architect; owner of the frontend after the initial AI scaffold; owner of infrastructure, data modelling, deployment and production operations.
portfolio_material.solution: NestJS modular monolith with a separated worker process; PostgreSQL via Prisma as single source of truth; idempotency enforced by database constraints rather than queue semantics; pricing and billing configuration held as data; a full audit log as the observability layer of last resort.

probable_rescue_defect.root_cause: const rawBody = req.rawBody || req.body || req; - the fallback silently passes parsed JSON or the entire request object into stripe.webhooks.constructEvent whenever the raw body is absent, guaranteeing signature failure AND suppressing the diagnostic signal
probable_rescue_defect.compounding_defect: Hand-rolled HMAC debug logging whose comparison prefixes 'v1=' onto one side while splitting it off the other, so it can never evaluate true - producing a false negative that would misdirect any developer or AI tool toward the secret or payload
probable_rescue_defect.rebuild_fix: app.use('/stripe/webhook', raw({ type: 'application/json' })) - one line, no fallback, nothing to mask failure
probable_rescue_defect.evidence_level: VERIFIED that both defects exist and that the rebuild handles it correctly; INFERRED that this is the specific defect fixed in 2025

commercial_status.correction_notice: An earlier revision of this dossier concluded there were NO paying customers. That was wrong. The flawed inference was: no 'stripe:invoice-credit:*' ledger entries exist, therefore no paid invoice was processed. The BASIC plan is configured with SUBSCRIPTION quill value = 0, so a paid BASIC invoice correctly produces no credit ledger entry. Absence of a derived record is not absence of the source event.
proof: 3 chargebacks of exactly 1499 USD minor units ($14.99) each, carrying genuine Stripe chargeId, paymentIntentId and stripeDisputeId - a chargeback cannot exist without a charge
83 invoices paid versus 44 subscriptions created: 39 invoices paid beyond the one-trial-invoice-per-subscription baseline, i.e. recurring renewals
101 invoice.payment_failed events, which only occur when a real card is charged
8 subscribers currently active, all past trial end, all BASIC monthly; longest continuously active 125 days
A customer's own words recorded in a dispute: 'I did not sign up for a plan but you charged me 14,99'
commercial_status.basic_plan_price_basis: All 3 chargebacks are exactly 1499 USD minor units; all 44 SubscriptionHistory rows are BASIC; all active subscribers are on MONTH interval; a customer independently quotes the same figure
commercial_status.estimated_gross_revenue_calculation: 39 invoices paid beyond trial baseline (83 paid - 44 subscriptions created) x $14.99
commercial_status.estimated_gross_revenue_qualification: The database does not store invoice amounts. Gross, before Stripe fees and before deducting $44.97 refunded in chargebacks. Upper bound if any subscription skipped its trial: 83 x $14.99 = $1,244. AUTHORITATIVE FIGURE IS IN THE STRIPE DASHBOARD - read it from there before citing. Treat as order of magnitude: hundreds of dollars, not thousands.
commercial_status.stripe_mode: Almost certainly LIVE - STRONGLY_SUPPORTED by genuine charge/payment-intent/dispute identifiers, sustained dunning, and a customer-reported charge. Production Stripe keys in the Render dashboard were not inspected.
commercial_status.career_framing: Cite the billing system's correctness under live money - 462 events deduplicated, 39 renewals, 101 dunning failures, 3 chargebacks correctly reversed - never the revenue amount. The system is commercially PROVEN but not commercially SIGNIFICANT.
